title: Give Responsibility for Disruptive Technologies to Organizations Whose Customers Need Them
coreMove: Place a disruptive effort with the team whose customers actually create pull toward it — not just the team with the relevant technical expertise.
sourcePressure: Organizations answer to the customers that fund their legitimacy. If a disruptive effort lives inside a unit whose customers don't need it, that unit will keep prioritizing what those customers reward — even with strong executive support. Placement changes which customers generate urgency and which priorities are real.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating this chapter as advice to always spin out every new effort into a separate company, when the rule is about customer fit, not corporate structure. An effort can be separate within a division or shared across a subsidiary — what matters is whose customers define success.

hook: generic 'build a startup inside your company' framing
counterintuition: generic 'leadership doesn't create culture, customers do' counter
tryThisNow: generic 'identify your internal innovation champion' prompt
examples: any scene that portrays separation as automatically winning
any scene where the wrong placement is simply blamed on a reluctant executive

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: Placement decisions are organizational, not heroic — open in the structural moment, not the announcement.

exampleSpecs.domain: hospital system placing a telemedicine program inside the inpatient unit versus the urgent-care division
exampleSpecs.audience: a hospital operations director deciding where to house a telemedicine pilot for non-emergency follow-up visits
exampleSpecs.stakes: the inpatient unit's customers are admitted patients who don't need telemedicine; the urgent-care division sees walk-in patients who might prefer remote follow-up
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Laura places the telemedicine pilot inside the inpatient unit because the technical infrastructure is there. Eighteen months later the pilot has produced nothing because no admitted patient needs what it offers — the urgent-care division, which does have patients who would use it, was never asked.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an empty telemedicine kiosk in a hospital corridor near the inpatient ward
mustInclude: the eighteen-month result from wrong placement
mustAvoid: implying that telemedicine is inherently better than in-person care

exampleSpecs.domain: retail bank housing its mobile peer-to-peer payment product inside the corporate banking division
exampleSpecs.audience: a product director who placed the mobile payment product under corporate banking because the technical compliance team is there
exampleSpecs.stakes: corporate banking customers have no need for P2P payment features; retail checking customers do, and they are in a different division
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ryan's product roadmap for mobile P2P is shaped entirely by corporate banking requirements — security audit cadence, API compliance, institutional transfer logic — because those are the customers who fund the division's decisions. The retail checking customers who would use P2P daily are in a division that doesn't control the roadmap.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a mobile payment product roadmap dominated by compliance milestones rather than user features
mustInclude: corporate compliance requirements dominating the roadmap
the structural explanation for why this happened
mustAvoid: suggesting that compliance requirements are unimportant

exampleSpecs.domain: broadcast media company housing its streaming studio inside the cable programming division
exampleSpecs.audience: a content strategy director whose streaming studio budget is approved by cable programming executives whose renewal metrics are based on cable subscriber counts
exampleSpecs.stakes: the cable programming division's customers are cable operators, not streaming subscribers — so the streaming studio keeps being asked to produce content that looks good on cable metrics
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Julien has to decide whether to produce a streaming-native format that will perform poorly on cable metrics or adapt it to cable's needs and lose the streaming advantage. The decision is structurally forced by which division controls the budget and who their customers are.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a content brief with two audience targets crossed out, one circled: cable subscribers
mustInclude: cable operator as customer of the division
mustAvoid: treating cable vs. streaming as a technology battle rather than an organizational placement problem

exampleSpecs.domain: commercial insurer housing its usage-based insurance product inside the actuarial division
exampleSpecs.audience: a product innovation director whose usage-based product sits inside actuarial because that's where the pricing models live
exampleSpecs.stakes: actuarial's customers are underwriters and claims directors who need long-run risk data — usage-based requires real-time behavioral data from drivers, which is a different kind of customer relationship
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Astrid predicts the usage-based product will be ready for market in two years based on actuarial's modeling timeline. The reveal shows that actuarial's modeling cycle was built for products whose customers send in one form per year, not products whose customers expect weekly app feedback. The customers the product needs created no pull inside the division that owned it.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an actuarial model timeline showing annual review cycles beside a driver app that refreshes weekly
mustInclude: the absence of driver-customer pull inside the actuarial division
mustAvoid: implying that actuarial modeling is wrong or outdated in general

exampleSpecs.domain: legacy retailer housing its subscription box service inside the merchandising department
exampleSpecs.audience: a merchandising director whose customers are wholesale buyers and store planners, not end consumers ordering personal curated boxes
exampleSpecs.stakes: merchandising's planning cycles are seasonal and bulk-volume; subscription box requires weekly curation and individual-level personalization that wholesale buyers never need
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Luca's postmortem on the failed subscription box pilot finds that the box was curated using wholesale buyer feedback — the only customer signal the merchandising team knew how to collect. The individual subscriber's preference data was never in the room.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a subscription box on a warehouse packing table beside a bulk wholesale order
mustInclude: wholesale buyer feedback as the only signal
the postmortem finding the root cause in organizational placement
mustAvoid: treating subscription boxes as inherently harder than traditional retail

exampleSpecs.domain: commercial printing company housing its on-demand digital printing service inside the offset plant management team
exampleSpecs.audience: a plant manager whose performance is measured by offset press utilization and long-run job efficiency
exampleSpecs.stakes: on-demand digital printing thrives on short-run variety; the plant manager's incentives push toward long-run standardization
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before: Min's on-demand service is scheduled around offset press priority — it runs when the offset presses don't need the floor space. After: the on-demand service is moved under the customer accounts team whose clients need quick turnaround, and scheduling decisions are now pulled by customer delivery dates rather than press utilization.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a plant scheduling board with on-demand jobs in the gap between long-run offset jobs
mustInclude: offset utilization metric as the scheduling driver
customer delivery date as the alternative driver
the explicit before/after in scheduling logic
mustAvoid: suggesting that offset printing is obsolete or that digital printing is always preferable

skillTargets: identify which customers are generating priority signals in a described organizational unit
recognize a placement where customer pull is pointing away from the disruptive effort
evaluate whether a described organizational placement creates customer fit or customer mismatch
apply the customer-fit principle to a described new product initiative
distinguish customer-fit placement from structural separation as the key variable

tryThisNowSpec: Name one new initiative in your organization and identify the team that currently owns it. Write down who that team's three most important customers are. Then write one sentence about whether those customers create pull toward or away from the initiative.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one research-aside or direct second-person paragraph about what 'customer pull' looks like in the reader's own organization
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
